Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

title: Final exam study guide
text:
Unit I — Vectors and geometry (Lectures 01–14)
Use the Midterm 1 study guide for the full outcome list. High-priority skills for the final:

Represent data as vectors; add, scale, and form linear combinations.
Compute and interpret inner products, norms, distances, RMS, angles, and cosine similarity.
Distinguish linear vs affine models; evaluate \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) in context.
Run a small nearest-neighbor or \(k\)-means step by hand and discuss scale.
Use dependence, span, subspace, basis, dimension, and orthonormal language accurately.

section: Unit II — Matrices, systems, and dynamics (Lectures 18–25)
text:
Unit II — Matrices, systems, and dynamics (Lectures 18–25)
Use the Midterm 2 study guide for the full outcome list. High-priority skills for the final:

Compute \(Ax\), interpret columns, and recognize common 2D transforms.
Translate contexts into \(Ax=b\); solve small systems; read RREF (pivots, free variables, consistency).
Model \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\); compute a few steps; relate \(A^k x\) to long-run behavior.
Multiply matrices; compose transforms; compare computational orders.
Use invertibility, rank, column space, null space, and \(2\times 2\) / triangular determinants.

title: Final exam study guide
text:
Unit III — Since Midterm 2 (Lectures 35–40)

Lecture 28 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair \((A,v,\lambda)\) by checking \(Av=\lambda v\).
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.



Lecture 29 — Characteristic equation, \(2\times 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors (including simple complex cases at the course’s level).
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.



Lecture 30 — Why did the system behave that way?

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors with software and verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\).
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain growth, decay, or approach to a direction.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation / oscillation behavior.
Observe orthogonal eigenvectors for a symmetric example when it appears.
Connect eigen-language back to earlier dynamical simulations.



Lecture 31 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) as the closest attainable vector in \(C(A)\).
Interpret the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.



Lecture 32 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness

Compute a least-squares solution with software (and check a tiny case by hand when asked).
Interpret residuals and RMS error in context.
Check that the residual is orthogonal to the columns of \(A\) (normal equations idea).
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, and positive definite when \(A\) has independent columns.
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful, not only report coefficients.



Lecture 33 — SVD, low-rank approximation, and capstone launch

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually (orthogonal factors + singular values).
Explain what a rank-\(k\) approximation keeps and what it discards.
Compare singular-value decay qualitatively for different data matrices.
Relate reconstruction error and storage to the choice of rank \(k\).
State a practical limitation of a low-rank model (what structure it may miss).

Each year: \(90\%\) of urban residents stay urban and \(10\%\) move rural; \(80\%\) of rural residents stay rural and \(20\%\) move urban. The transition matrix (columns = “from”) is \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}}.
\] If \(\mathbf{x}_0=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(\mathbf{x}_1=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_0\) and interpret the two entries.
B22. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\ 0.5&0.5\end{bmatrix}}.
\] For the system \(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_t\), express \(\mathbf{x}_3\) in terms of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{x}_0\) using a matrix power (do not expand unless you want to check).
B23. Two rooms: each day, \(70\%\) in Room A stay and \(30\%\) move to B; \(60\%\) in B stay and \(40\%\) move to A. Let \(\mathbf{x}_t=(a,\mathbf{b})\).

Write \(\mathbf{A}\) so \(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}x_t\) (columns = from).
If \(\mathbf{x}_0=(50,50)\), compute \(\mathbf{x}_1\).
Does total occupancy stay \(100\)?



Matrix products and powers
B24. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}},\quad
\mathbf{B}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Compute \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\). Are they equal?
B25. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Compute \(\mathbf{A}^2\).
B26. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Compute \(\mathbf{A}^2\) and \(\mathbf{A}^3\). Guess a formula for \(\mathbf{A}^k\).
B27. Let \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix}}\). Compute \(\mathbf{A}^2\) and \(\mathbf{A}^3\). Guess \(\mathbf{A}^k\).
B28. Let \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix}}\). Compute \(\mathbf{A}^2\) and \(\mathbf{A}^3 \mathbf{x}\) for \(\mathbf{x}=(1,1)\). Relate to two steps of \(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}x_t\).


Inverses
B29. Find \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) (if it exists) by reducing \([\mathbf{A}\mid \mathbf{I}]\) to \([\mathbf{I}\mid \mathbf{A}^{-1}]\): \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
B30. Is \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}}
\] invertible? Give two different reasons (determinant or null space).
B31. Solve \[
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\ x_2\end{bmatrix}}
=
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}3\\ 2\end{bmatrix}}
\] without forming an inverse explicitly.
B32. Use the \(2\times 2\) formula to invert \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 2&3\end{bmatrix}}\). Check \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\).
B33. Suppose reducing \([\mathbf{A}\mid \mathbf{I}]\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix yields \[
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&3&-1\\ 0&1&|&-2&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\] What is \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\)? What was \(\det \mathbf{A}\) if \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\ 2&3\end{bmatrix}}\)?


Rank, column space, null space
B34. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Describe \(C(\mathbf{A})\). Is \(\mathbf{b}=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(\mathbf{A})\)? Is \(\mathbf{b}=(1,3,0)\) in \(C(\mathbf{A})\)?
B35. Let \[
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Find \(N(\mathbf{A})\). Give a basis for \(N(\mathbf{A})\), or state that only \(0\) is in the null space.
B36. The RREF of a \(3\times 4\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \[
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\)? Which original columns form a basis for \(C(\mathbf{A})\) (pivot columns)? Find a basis for \(N(\mathbf{A})\).
B37. The RREF of a \(3\times 4\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is \[
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}}.
\] What is \(\dim N(\mathbf{A})\)? Check \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})+\dim N(\mathbf{A})=n\).
B38. Let \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\ 2&4&6\end{bmatrix}}\).

Find \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\).
Find a basis for \(C(\mathbf{A})\) and for \(N(\mathbf{A})\).
Is \(\mathbf{b}=(1,2)\) in \(C(\mathbf{A})\)? Is \(\mathbf{b}=(1,3)\)?



Determinants
B39. Compute \[
\det\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
B40. Compute \[
\det\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&1&0\\ 0&-3&4\\ 0&0&5\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
B41. The map \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\ 0&3\end{bmatrix}}\) sends the unit square to a rectangle. What is the area of that rectangle? How does this relate to \(\det \mathbf{A}\)?
B42. Solve by elimination: \[
\begin{aligned}
x-y&=1,\\
2x+y&=5.
\end{aligned}
\] How many solutions?
B43. The RREF of \([\mathbf{A}\mid \mathbf{b}]\) is \[
\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & | & 4 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}}.
\] Write the general solution. What is \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\)?
B44. Let \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\ 0&1&1\end{bmatrix}}\).

Find a basis for \(C(\mathbf{A})\) and state \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\).
Find a basis for \(N(\mathbf{A})\).
Check rank–nullity.

B45. Compute \(\det\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&5\end{bmatrix}}\) and, if possible, \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) by the \(2\times 2\) formula.

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
C. Word problems
Show your work. Write equations and matrices carefully, then interpret the final answer in context.
C1. A campus coffee cart sells only lattes and drip coffee. On Monday the cart sold 120 drinks and took in $430. Lattes cost $4 each and drip coffee costs $3 each. Let \(x\) be the number of lattes sold and \(y\) the number of drip coffees sold.

Write a system of two linear equations for \(x\) and \(y\).
Write the system as an augmented matrix \([\mathbf{A}\,|\,\mathbf{b}]\).
Use elementary row operations (no row swaps needed) to put the augmented matrix into echelon form.
Solve for \(x\) and \(y\).
State the answer in context (how many of each drink were sold).

C2. A food truck makes two burrito fillings. Each order of filling A uses 2 cups of beans and 1 cup of rice. Each order of filling B uses 1 cup of beans and 3 cups of rice. Today the truck has 16 cups of beans and 13 cups of rice to use completely. Let \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) be the number of orders of A and B.

Write the system as \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) (give \(\mathbf{A}\), \(\mathbf{x}\), and \(\mathbf{b}\)).
Using elementary matrices / row operations, clear below the first pivot to reach an upper-triangular \(\mathbf{U}\). Write the elementary matrix \(\mathbf{E}\) for that step and check \(\mathbf{E}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\).
Invert \(\mathbf{E}\) to get \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{E}^{-1}\), and verify \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}\).
Solve \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}\) by forward substitution, then \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}\) by back substitution.
State how many orders of each filling the truck should make.

C3. Two dorm buildings, North and South, share a shuttle. Each week: 80% of North residents stay North and 20% move South; 70% of South residents stay South and 30% move North. Let \(\mathbf{x}_t=(n_t,s_t)\) be the number of residents in North and South at the start of week \(t\).

Write the transition matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) so that \(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_t\) (columns = “from”).
If \(\mathbf{x}_0=(200,100)\), compute \(\mathbf{x}_1=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_0\).
Does the total number of residents stay \(300\)? Briefly why, in terms of \(\mathbf{A}\) or the story.
Express \(\mathbf{x}_2\) using a matrix power (you need not multiply it out).

C4. A workshop runs two machines. If \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\) is hours on machine 1 and machine 2, the output is \[
\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x},\qquad
\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 2&4\end{bmatrix}},
\] where \(\mathbf{y}=(\text{parts},\text{scrap})\).

From \(\mathbf{A}\), find a basis for the column space \(C(\mathbf{A})\) and a basis for the null space \(N(\mathbf{A})\).
Sketch \(C(\mathbf{A})\) and \(N(\mathbf{A})\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (both are subspaces through the origin — say what geometric object each is).
State \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})\) and \(\dim N(\mathbf{A})\), and check that rank–nullity holds for this \(2\times 2\) matrix.
In one sentence: what does (b)+(c) say about which output vectors \(\mathbf{y}\) are possible, and about uniqueness of \(\mathbf{x}\) when a solution exists?

title: Math 107 Midterm 2 practice
text:
Answers
Check only after a closed-book attempt. Update your definitions/formulas list for every miss.

A — Definitions (key points)
A1. \(\mathbf{A}\) has \(m\) rows and \(n\) columns; each column is an \(m\)-vector.
A2. \(A_{ij}\) is the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\); \(\mathbf{a}_j\) is the \(j\)th column of \(\mathbf{A}\). Here \(A_{12}=-1\) and \(\mathbf{a}_2=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}}\).
A3. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=x_1 \mathbf{a}_1+\cdots+x_n \mathbf{a}_n\).
A4. Input \(\mathbf{x}\), output \(\mathbf{y}\), transform \(\mathbf{A}\). Size of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(m\times n\).
A5. \(\mathbf{A}\): triangular. \(\mathbf{B}\): identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric. \(\mathbf{C}\): sparse.
A6. \(\mathbf{b}\in C(\mathbf{A})\) (equivalently: \(\mathbf{b}\) is a linear combination of the columns).
A7. Upper-left; pivot; \(1\); below; diagonal; above; below; lower-right.
A8. \(\mathbf{R}_1\): yes. \(\mathbf{R}_2\): no — not reduced (nonzero entry above the pivot in column 2). \(\mathbf{R}_3\): no — pivot in row 2 is \(2\), not \(1\).
A9. Pivot: \(x_1,x_2\). Free: \(x_3\).
A10. 1–b, 2–c, 3–a.
A11. \(\mathbf{x}_{t+1}=\mathbf{A}x_t\); \(\mathbf{x}_t\) is the state, \(\mathbf{A}\) is the transition / update matrix.
A12. Inner dimensions match (\(\mathbf{A}\)’s columns \(=\) \(\mathbf{B}\)’s rows); \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) is \(m\times p\).
A13. Order matters: \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}\) need not both be defined, and even when both are, they need not be equal.
A14. \(\mathbf{x}_k=\mathbf{A}^k \mathbf{x}_0\) (after \(k\) steps).
A15. There exists \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{I}\). For square \(\mathbf{A}\), invertible iff \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a unique solution for every \(\mathbf{b}\).
A16. \(C(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\); \(N(\mathbf{A})=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=0\}\).
A17. \(n=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})+\dim N(\mathbf{A})\) (equivalently \(n=\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})+\operatorname{nullity}(\mathbf{A})\)).
A18. \(ad-bc\); absolute value \(=\) area scaling factor for the unit square (signed area accounts for orientation).
A19. False — \(\det \mathbf{A}=0\) means noninvertible.
A20. Independent spanning list; dimension \(=\) number of vectors in any basis.
A21. (a) \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}}\) (b) \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-3\end{bmatrix}}\) (c) \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 2&1\end{bmatrix}}\)
A22. \(\mathbf{E}_1\): multiply row 2 by \(5\). \(\mathbf{E}_2\): swap the two rows. \(\mathbf{E}_3\): add \(4\) times row 2 to row 1.
A23. \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\ -c&a\end{bmatrix}}\); division by zero / no inverse when \(\det \mathbf{A}=0\).
A24. (a) \(m\)-vector (b) \(m\times n\) matrix (c) undefined — inner dimensions \(3\neq 2\) (d) \(n\times m\) matrix (e) scalar (f) undefined — singular, no inverse (g) set of vectors (h) set of vectors (i) scalar (nonnegative integer) (j) undefined — \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}\) sizes fail (k) \(2\)-vector (l) \(m\)-vector that is the zero vector when consistent (m) \(2\times 3\) matrix (n) scalar equal to \(3\) (\(n-\operatorname{rank}=5-2\))
A25. False — \(N(\mathbf{A})=\{0\}\) gives uniqueness when a solution exists, but \(\mathbf{b}\) might miss \(C(\mathbf{A})\) (e.g. tall full-column-rank \(\mathbf{A}\)).
A26. 1–a, 2–b, 3–a, 4–a, 5–a.
A27. Fraction (or amount) moving from state \(j\) into state \(i\) in one step.


B — Easy computations
B1. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=2\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}}+1\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 3\end{bmatrix}}+(-1)\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\end{bmatrix}}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}}\).
B2. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}4\\ -5\end{bmatrix}}\).
B3. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 3\\ -2\end{bmatrix}}\).
B4. Input \(\mathbf{x}\) is \(3\times 1\) (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)); output \(\mathbf{y}\) is \(2\times 1\) (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)).
B5. \(\mathbf{y}_1=(0,1)\), \(\mathbf{y}_2=(-1,0)\); sketch shows basis vectors rotated \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise. Effect of \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\): \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation.
B6. \(\mathbf{y}_1=(1,0)\), \(\mathbf{y}_2=(2,1)\); sketch shows \(\mathbf{x}_1\) fixed and \(\mathbf{x}_2\) sent to \((2,1)\). Effect of \(\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\): shear (horizontal shear).
B7. \(\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}}\); \(2\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\ 0&6\end{bmatrix}}\); \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}=\mathbf{A}\).
B8. Symmetric: yes. Triangular: no. Diagonal: no.
B9. \(\mathbf{D}\mathbf{F}\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 2\end{bmatrix}}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-2\\ 1\end{bmatrix}}\).
B10. \(\mathbf{A}^{\mathsf{T}}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\ 0&1\\ 2&0\end{bmatrix}}\), size \(3\times 2\).
B11. \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0&0&-1\\ 0&1&0\end{bmatrix}}\).
B12. \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 3&-1\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}x\\ y\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{b}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}5\\ 1\end{bmatrix}}\).
B13. Unique solution: \(\mathbf{x}=1\), \(y=2\).
B14. Pivots \(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2\); free \(\mathbf{x}_3=t\). General: \(\mathbf{x}=(3-2t,\ 1+t,\ t)\).
B15. No solutions — inconsistent (\(0=4\)).
B16. RREF \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}}\); infinitely many: \(\mathbf{x}_1=3-2t\), \(\mathbf{x}_2=t\).
B17. No — second row of \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(2\times\) first, but \(7\neq 2\cdot 3\).
B18. Pivot vars \(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_3\); free \(\mathbf{x}_2=s\), \(\mathbf{x}_4=t\); rank \(2\); yes consistent; \[
\mathbf{x}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 0\\ -1\\ 0\end{bmatrix}}+s\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-3\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}}+t\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 0\\ -4\\ 1\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
B19. Result \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}}\); infinitely many: \(\mathbf{x}_1=3-2t\), \(\mathbf{x}_2=t\).
B20. \(\mathbf{x}_1=(0.5,0.5)\); \(\mathbf{x}_2=(0.5,0.5)\).
B21. \(\mathbf{x}_1=(0.62,0.38)\); urban / rural fractions tomorrow.
B22. \(\mathbf{x}_3=\mathbf{A}^3 \mathbf{x}_0\).
B23. (a) \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.4\\ 0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix}}\). (b) \(\mathbf{x}_1=(55,45)\). (c) Yes — total \(100\).
B24. \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&0\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 1&2\end{bmatrix}}\); not equal.
B25. \(\mathbf{A}^2=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}\).
B26. \(\mathbf{A}^2=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{A}^3=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}\); \(\mathbf{A}^k=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}\).
B27. \(\mathbf{A}^2=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\ 0&9\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{A}^3=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}8&0\\ 0&27\end{bmatrix}}\); \(\mathbf{A}^k=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2^k&0\\ 0&3^k\end{bmatrix}}\).
B28. \(\mathbf{A}^2=0\), so \(\mathbf{A}^3 \mathbf{x}=0\); after two steps the state is already \(0\) (same as \(\mathbf{x}_2=\mathbf{A}^2 \mathbf{x}_0\)).
B29. \([\mathbf{A}\mid \mathbf{I}]=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&1&0\\ 0&1&|&0&1\end{bmatrix}}\to\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&1&-2\\ 0&1&|&0&1\end{bmatrix}}\), so \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}}\).
B30. Not invertible: \(\det=0\); nontrivial null space, e.g. \((2,-1)\).
B31. \(\mathbf{x}_2=2\), \(\mathbf{x}_1=1\).
B32. \(\det=1\); \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\ -2&1\end{bmatrix}}\); product is \(\mathbf{I}\).
B33. \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\ -2&1\end{bmatrix}}\); \(\det \mathbf{A}=1\).
B34. \(C(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(0,0,1)\}=\{(\mathbf{x},2\mathbf{x},z)\}\). \((1,2,3)\): yes; \((1,3,0)\): no.
B35. \(N(\mathbf{A})=\{0\}\) (two pivot columns).
B36. Rank \(2\); pivot columns 1 and 3. Free \(\mathbf{x}_2=s\), \(\mathbf{x}_4=t\): \[
\mathbf{x}=s\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-2\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0\end{bmatrix}}+t\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-3\\ 0\\ 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}}.
\]
B37. \(\dim N(\mathbf{A})=2\); \(2+2=4=n\).
B38. (a) Rank \(1\). (b) \(C(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)\}\); \(N(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,0),(-3,0,1)\}\). (c) \((1,2)\) yes; \((1,3)\) no.
B39. \(12-2=10\).
B40. Product of diagonal: \(2\cdot(-3)\cdot 5=-30\).
B41. Area \(6\); equals \(|\det \mathbf{A}|=6\).
B42. Unique: \(\mathbf{x}=2\), \(y=1\).
B43. Free \(\mathbf{x}_2=t\); \(\mathbf{x}=(4-2t,\ t,\ -1)\); \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})=2\).
B44. (a) Columns span \(\mathbb{R}^2\); e.g. basis \(\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\) or the first two columns; rank \(2\). (b) \(N(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(-1,1,-1)\}\) (equivalently \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,1)\}\)). (c) \(2+1=3=n\).
B45. \(\det=1\cdot5-2\cdot3=-1\); \(\mathbf{A}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}-5&2\\ 3&-1\end{bmatrix}}\).


C — Word problems
C1. (a) \(x+y=120\), \(4x+3y=430\). (b) \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1&|&120\\ 4&3&|&430\end{bmatrix}}\). (c) e.g. \(R_2\leftarrow R_2-4R_1\) gives \(\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&1&|&120\\ 0&-1&|&-50\end{bmatrix}}\) (echelon). (d) \(y=50\), \(x=70\). (e) 70 lattes and 50 drip coffees.
C2. (a) \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 1&3\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,x_2)\), \(\mathbf{b}=(16,13)\). (b) Subtract \(\tfrac12\) times row 1 from row 2: \(\mathbf{E}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ -1/2&1\end{bmatrix}}\), \(\mathbf{U}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\ 0&5/2\end{bmatrix}}\). (c) \(\mathbf{L}=\mathbf{E}^{-1}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 1/2&1\end{bmatrix}}\); \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{A}\). (d) \(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}\) gives \(\mathbf{y}=(16,5)\); \(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}\) gives \(x_2=2\), \(x_1=7\). (e) 7 orders of A and 2 orders of B.
C3. (a) \(\mathbf{A}=\boldsymbol{\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.3\\ 0.2&0.7\end{bmatrix}}\). (b) \(\mathbf{x}_1=(190,110)\). (c) Yes — total \(300\) (each column of \(\mathbf{A}\) sums to \(1\), so totals are preserved). (d) \(\mathbf{x}_2=\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{x}_0\).
C4. (a) \(C(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)\}\) (second column \(=2\times\) first); \(N(\mathbf{A})=\operatorname{span}\{(2,-1)\}\) (solve \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}=0\)). (b) \(C(\mathbf{A})\): the line through the origin in direction \((1,2)\). \(N(\mathbf{A})\): the line through the origin in direction \((2,-1)\). (c) \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A})=1\), \(\dim N(\mathbf{A})=1\), and \(1+1=2=n\). (d) Possible outputs \(\mathbf{y}\) lie only on that line in the \((\text{parts},\text{scrap})\)-plane; when \(\mathbf{y}\) is achievable, \(\mathbf{x}\) is not unique (you can add any multiple of \((2,-1)\)).

text:
Learning outcomes (Lectures 18–25)

Light review — Quiz 5 / basis (Lecture 14)

Explain what a basis accomplishes and what dimension means.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use span, independence, basis, and dimension accurately when they reappear with matrices (column space, null space, rank).



Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects

Identify matrix dimensions, rows, columns, and entries.
Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.



Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.



Lecture 20 — Transforming space

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply a transform matrix to given points by hand.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.
Sketch or describe the image of simple shapes under a stated transform.



Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination

Translate equations into \(Ax=b\) and classify the system as square, overdetermined, or underdetermined.
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) is in the span of the columns; anticipate no solution, one solution, or infinitely many.
Match each elementary row operation with its matrix, use those matrices to eliminate, and solve a small system by back substitution.
Explain why those row operations preserve the solution set.



Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems

Read a reduced row echelon form: name pivot and free variables and write a parametric solution.
Tell inconsistent, unique, and infinitely many solutions apart from that form.
Write an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) and build the transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next state or two.



Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products

Apply an elementary matrix to an augmented matrix and read the solution set (including a parametric form).
Classify unique / none / infinitely many from RREF and write infinite families with a parameter \(t\).
Build a transition matrix from a two-compartment flow and compute one step \(x_1=Ax_0\).
Explain why two steps need \(A(Ax_0)\) / \(A^2\), and compute a small product \(AB\) by hand.
Give an example with \(AB\neq BA\), and compute \(A^2\) and a small power \(A^n x\).



Lecture 24 — Inverses, rank, and solvability

Explain why reducing \([A\mid I]\) to \([I\mid B]\) gives \(B=A^{-1}\), and use an inverse to solve \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(C(A)\) as possible outputs and \(N(A)\) as inputs sent to zero.
Find rank from pivots and use \(\dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
Explain when \(Ax=b\) is solvable and when a solution is unique.
Distinguish square invertibility from full column rank for a tall matrix.



Lecture 25 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.

This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

Wed Nov 4 — Inverses, rank, and solvability
Lecture 24 page
Reading: Boyd 11.1–11.3; class notes + selected Strang §3.5 (rank, \(C(A)\), \(N(A)\)); Lab 3 peek.
Why in this course: Inverse = undo map when \(A\) is square and full rank. \(C(A)\) / \(N(A)\) / rank = solvability and uniqueness language for general \(A\) (including rectangular / singular). Not a four-subspaces theory unit.
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain why reducing \([A\mid I]\) to \([I\mid B]\) gives \(B=A^{-1}\), and use an inverse to solve \(Ax=b\).
Interpret \(C(A)\) as possible outputs and \(N(A)\) as inputs sent to zero.
Find rank from pivots and use \(\dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
Explain when \(Ax=b\) is solvable and when a solution is unique.
Distinguish square invertibility from full column rank for a tall matrix.
